Corporate Prayer
KOR-puh-rit PRAIR
noun phrase
From Latin corporatus (united into one body, from corpus, body) and Old English præger (prayer, petition, from Late Latin precaria, obtained by entreaty, from prex, prayer, petition). The term renders the New Testament pattern of the gathered ekklesia lifting its voice together to the Father — a practice evidenced from the upper room (Acts 1:14) through the apostolic church (Acts 4:24) and commanded in the Pauline epistles (Eph. 6:18).

Biblical Definition

Corporate prayer is the gathered covenant community’s united address to God in the assembly — distinct from but complementary to the private prayer of the individual saint. The New Testament establishes the pattern unmistakably. In Acts 1:14, the 120 disciples “with one mind were continually devoting themselves to prayer” before Pentecost. When Peter was imprisoned, “prayer was being made fervently by the church to God” on his behalf (Acts 12:5). When the Jerusalem church heard the Sanhedrin's threats, “they lifted their voices to God with one accord” (Acts 4:24) — and the place where they were assembled was shaken. Paul commands that “with all prayer and petition” believers pray “at all times in the Spirit,” including “petition for all the saints” (Eph. 6:18) — a communal, not merely individual, discipline.

Christ Himself established the principle when He said, “Where two or three have gathered together in My name, there I am in their midst” (Matt. 18:20). The Lord's Prayer is given in the first-person plural (“Our Father”) — a corporate form even when prayed individually. Reformed ecclesiology recognizes corporate prayer as an indispensable mark of the healthy church: it is where the body confesses its dependence upon God, intercedes for the saints and for the lost, gives thanks for grace received, and aligns its will with the sovereign purposes of the King. The prayer meeting is not a second-tier activity reserved for the especially devout; it is the church doing what the church exists to do — cry out to its Maker in one voice.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defined prayer as “in a general sense, the act of asking for a favor, and particularly with earnestness; a petition or earnest request.” Corporate adds the communal dimension: the gathered body asking in concert, not merely the individual in private.

expand to see more

PRAYER, n. [L. precarius; Fr. prière; from L. precor, to pray, to ask.]

In a general sense, the act of asking for a favor, and particularly with earnestness. In a specific sense, a solemn address to the Supreme Being, consisting of adoration, confession, supplication, and thanksgiving.

A petition; an earnest request or entreaty. The publick or social worship of God by prayer, as distinguished from private devotion.

In theology, prayer is the direct address of the creature to the Creator, the soul's confession of dependence and desire for communion with God; it requires faith in the existence, perfection, and covenant relationship of the God addressed.

CORPORATE, adj. [L. corporatus, corpus, body.] United in a body; formed into a body politic. Applied to prayer: the united, assembled petition of the gathered community as a single body, not individual voices merely coinciding.

Key Scripture

Acts 1:14 — "These all continued with one accord in prayer and supplication, with the women, and Mary the mother of Jesus, and with his brethren."

Acts 4:24 — "And when they heard that, they lifted up their voice to God with one accord, and said, Lord, thou art God, which hast made heaven, and earth, and the sea, and all that in them is:"

Matt. 18:20 — "For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them."

Eph. 6:18 — "Praying always with all prayer and supplication in the Spirit, and watching thereunto with all perseverance and supplication for all saints;"

Modern Corruption

Evangelical pragmatism has privatized prayer into a personal therapeutic practice, stripping corporate prayer of its ecclesiological weight and reducing the prayer meeting to an optional supplement.

expand to see more

The dominant corruption of corporate prayer in modern evangelical culture is the individualization and privatization of the entire practice. Under the influence of Pietism and revivalism, prayer became essentially a one-on-one transaction between the individual and God — personal devotions, quiet time, the “prayer closet” — while the gathered corporate prayer meeting withered. Charles Finney's 19th-century revivalism accelerated this: prayer was a technique for producing conversion results, not the corporate cry of the covenant community to its sovereign God. The result is that in most evangelical churches today, the corporate prayer meeting — once called “the thermometer of the church” — is the least attended gathering. The church that cannot gather to pray together has lost its first love (Rev. 2:4).

A secondary corruption is the charismatic misuse of corporate prayer as a performance or spiritual atmosphere machine — tongues-heavy, prophetically driven, experience-oriented gatherings where the goal is a felt “presence” rather than covenant communion with the God who hears petition. The biblical pattern is ordered, intelligible, Spirit-sustained corporate address to God — plain speech that the whole congregation can follow and affirm (1 Cor. 14:16). The Regulative Principle applies to prayer as to all else in corporate worship: God prescribes its character, and the church obeys.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Latin roots of both words point to the gathered body united in earnest petition before God — one body, one voice, one need.

expand to see more

Latin corpus (body) — the root from which corporate derives; in ecclesiology, the corpus Christi is the body of Christ, the gathered community whose united voice constitutes the corporate act

Latin prex, precis (prayer, entreaty) — the root of prayer; related to precarious (obtained by entreaty) and deprecate (to pray against); the sense is of earnest, dependent asking

Latin precaria (obtained by petition) — entering Old French as preiere and Middle English as prayere; the word carries the freight of petition made from a position of dependence

Greek proseuche (προσευχή) — prayer in the New Testament; also used of the place of prayer (Acts 16:13); the word is built from pros (toward) + euche (a wish or vow), meaning to direct one's wish toward God

Old English gebed (prayer, petition) — the pre-Latinate English word for prayer, carrying the sense of beseeching; the Latin term prevailed in ecclesiastical usage and gave English its standard word for the discipline

Usage

"The Westminster Directory for Public Worship (1645) gave detailed instructions for corporate prayer precisely because the Reformers understood that prayer is not merely a private grace but a public, ordered, covenantal act of the assembled church."

"Charles Spurgeon famously called the Metropolitan Tabernacle prayer meeting “the power house of the church” — the recognition that corporate prayer is not a supplement to ministry but its indispensable engine."

"When the early church faced the Sanhedrin's threats (Acts 4), it did not respond with a strategy committee; it gathered for prayer — and received fresh boldness by the Spirit, a pattern the church is meant to replicate in every generation of opposition."
